utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Mr. Bezruchenko, the affirmation you made still applies --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [French on English channel]... for some reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I have the same problem, Mr. Bezruchenko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We have French on channel 4; English I found on channel [Realtime transcript read in error "incompetent"] 3, if it helps. Hopefully, we will resolve ourselves very shortly.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Are you receiving the English translation Mr. Bezruchenko?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And I would start, Mr. Bezruchenko, by passing on to you a warning I have received yesterday from the interpreters. They have asked both of us to try to pause between questions and answers as it makes their work more difficult if we don't.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. Perhaps, I would suggest, I think what could resolve the problem somehow is that some parallel interpretation could be made so somebody could appropriately advise us on the pauses to be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, thank you for that. We will try, for the time being, to police ourselves, if we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can I observe as an outsider, you each have a tendency to become involved in the subject and to become excited even, and the more involved and the more excited each of you become, the quicker you come in your speech and the quicker you're ready to speak at the end of the other's conversation, and that reaches a point where it is beyond the capacity of the interpreters to keep up with you. And while that is happening, could I merely observe that at line 13, I wasn't speaking and I did not use the word "incompetent," speaking of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: We'll try to keep the excitement under control, Your Honour. Could the witness please be is shown what is exhibit P481, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, as you will see, this is the same document that we finished with last night. There are simply two more matters which I would like to draw your attention upon. The first one is in the first paragraph of that document, and you will recall that I had asked you whether the president in a number of documents referred to the NLA as a terrorist group or as terrorists. I would simply draw your attention to paragraph 1, and can you agree that the NLA in that paragraph is referred to as terrorist groups? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And drawing your attention to paragraph 4 of that particular document, do you agree, Mr. Bezruchenko, that one of the instructions or order that the president gave in relation to this matter was for the Chief of Staff of the army to report directly to him in relation to the matters mentioned in the previous paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown what is Exhibit 1D99, please. And, for the record, the document is to be found under tab 21 of the OTP binder of documents for Mr. Bezruchenko.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Briefly, Mr. Bezruchenko, two matters in relation to this order. Do you agree that the order is addressed to the Defence Command of the City of Skopje? Do you agree with that? It's on the top left-hand corner, I believe.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not really. I don't think it is addressed formally to the Command for the Defence of the City of Skopje. What it really says is that the subject of the document is formation of the command for the defence of the city of Skopje. This is the left upper corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And do you agree that this particular decision, as it is called, is then submitted to the Cabinet of the President of the Republic, and to the General Staff of the army?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: and perhaps the registry could scroll down for Mr. Bezruchenko, to the very bottom the document, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And do you agree that, again, this document is not submitted to the Ministry of Defence. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that the document is actually delivered to the Cabinet of the President of the Republic of Macedonia and to the Chief of the General Staff -- or to the General Staff of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And if the witness may now be shown Exhibit 1D58, please, this is tab 17 of the OTP binder. It's under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, this is, again, a document that you were shown by the Office of the Prosecutor in your examination-in-chief, and you've made already a number of comments upon it. But what I would like you to confirm is it's, again, a decision of the President of the Republic of Macedonia, Mr. Trajkovski, dated the 4th of June of 2001, and the subject heading is "The use of the Army of the Republic of Macedonia to carry out an operation." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly, sir. The appropriate word in Macedonian is use of the army for the getting out one operation. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And, as with the previous document, this particular decision of the president is, again, submitted to the Cabinet of the President, to the General Staff of the army of the Republic, but not to the Ministry of Defence. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, simply for the record, and to speed things up, we also draw your attention to Exhibit 1D50 and 1D52.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is it correct, Mr. Bezruchenko, that the president, as Commander in Chief of the army, could exercise his authority at any and every level of the hierarchy?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Macedonian Law on Defence adopted in 2001, to the best of my recollection, does not really specify this particular point; but I would imagine that in his capacity, as the Commander in Chief of the army, the president had the decisive and final authority as how the army should be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And that would be true, for instance, of mobilisation orders. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If I recall correctly, Article 18 of the New Law adopted in June 2001 specified that one of the powers of the president, in his capacity of the Commander in Chief, was, in fact, to call up mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And simply to conclude with this particular point, the president also had the power to decide what sort of army units -- what category of army unit should be mobilised in any particular circumstances. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not really give a definite "yes" or "no" answer to this question because, apparently, such issues would be decided on the expert level in General Staff, or on Ministry of Defence for that matter; but I would imagine that, again, in his capacity of the Commander in Chief, president would be closely involved there such matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I can show you a document, in that case, that may be useful?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: It is Exhibit P479, please. It's at tab 23 of the Prosecution binder of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Bezruchenko, this is a document that you are familiar with. You have been shown the document in your evidence-in-chief. Do you agree that this is one of the order of the president of the Republic of Macedonia, this one dated the 13th of June of 2001, and it orders, in paragraph 1, the mobilisation of certain army formations? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And the president orders that the mobilisation of this army structures or formations included, for instance, a platoon, a company, a battalion, a brigade, and a division of various categories. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. Mettraux, with the exception of division. I believe this is not a [indiscernible] battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, I think the transcript missed one word that you have said before battalion.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: An artillery battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'm grateful. Is it correct that in a number of orders and decisions, which the president issued in relation to what he called anti-terrorists operation, he exercised, in effect, what you called the operational aspects of the operations, whilst attributing to the Ministry of Defence solely logistical or financial obligations. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that would appear so.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, simply for the record, this would Exhibit P476, P477, P478, Exhibit 1D100, Exhibit P479. They are all part of the Prosecution binder of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is it correct that in a number of orders that the president -- or decisions that the president issued, he, in fact, went into quite a great detail regarding operational matters, including by selecting the type of weapons or armaments to be used in some operations? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think there is documentary evidence to this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, there would be, for instance, Exhibit P477, which is -- I apologise, P478, exhibit, which is at tab 20 of the Prosecution binder, and Exhibit P479, which is at tab 23 of the Prosecution binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is it also correct that in a number of orders or decisions issued by the president, the president himself decided on what troops should be deployed, as well as the timing of this deployment? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could answer this question, Mr. Mettraux, provided you substantiate it with a document related to these issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, perhaps we can stay with the document that's on your screen, to facilitate an expedite things, Mr. Bezruchenko. Is it correct that, in this particular occasion, the president identified the specific units, or army formations as we've called them, that should be mobilised, and he also indicated the time at which mobilisation should be taking place? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. But you will probably note the difference between the formulation of your previous question and this current question. In the previous question, you mentioned deployment of troops. In this current question, you speak about mobilisation. Obviously, these are two different things. If I may offer my detailed comments on this document, I would rather suggest that this document deals with mobilisation of the units and these units are precisely specified. This decision does not speak about deployment of these specific units anywhere in any region of Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'm grateful for the specification, Mr. Bezruchenko. Is it correct also that earlier on in your evidence-in-chief, you have indicated that, in your view, the mobilisation of troops would be relevant to what you termed operational control? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be relevant, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that the president of the Republic of Macedonia issued orders regarding anti-terrorists operations, as he termed them, all through the crisis, up to the time before the Ohrid Framework Agreement? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the decisions of the president regarding what was termed as "anti-terrorist operations" were actually interspaced in time between January, February, and August 2001, whereas, in fact, mobilisation continued well beyond this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bezruchenko. At this stage, I'm more interested in the first category of orders and decisions which you have identified. For instance, do you recall the, I think it's termed, resolution or decision of the 5th of August 2001, signed by the president which I showed a moment ago? Do you recall that document?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And do you recall that the resolution or decision concerned a necessary structure and force to enter the town of Tetovo with the aim of preventing its fall into the hands of the terrorist group, the self-styled NLA? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I please take a look at the document again.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown exhibit P481, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, this is the document with which started this morning.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And the passage I was reading to you a moment ago, Mr. Bezruchenko, is to be found in paragraph 1 of this document.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And you can confirm also that the date of this particular resolution or decision is the 5th of August, 2001. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Could the witness also be shown what is Exhibit 1D52, which is under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Do you have that decision in front of you, Mr. Bezruchenko?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Can you see a decision dated the 7th of August of 2001, signed by the President of the Republic of Macedonia, Mr. Trajkovski?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is it possible to magnify this document a little bit on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Perhaps, starting with the bottom left-hand corner of this document, Mr. Bezruchenko, can you see that this particular decision, as it's called, comes from the President of the Republic of Macedonia, that it is dated the 7th of August of 2001, and that it's a decision based on Article 79(2) of the Constitution of the Republic of Macedonia. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And if I can draw your attention to paragraph 1 of that particular decision, I will read it out to you. It says this: "In order to the army to respond accordingly and in due course with fire to the terrorist positions, every time when there is an attack on the security forces of the Republic of Macedonia and when that action is of danger to their lives. I underline that the measure taken by the army also includes instances when the members of the Ministry of Interior are in danger from the attacks." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And do you agree that, once again, the president of the republic refers to the NLA, or at least to their positions, as terrorist positions? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he does.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And what in effect the president order in this particular instance is to provide or to order the army to provide fire support or at least fire cover for the members of the Ministry of Interior, should they come in -- should they become in danger from attack. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And if I can draw you're attention to the last sentence of the second paragraph, it says this: "The army headquarters will report to me for every response with fire no later than three hours after the completed actions." So you agree that, once again, the president is ordering the army to report to him directly about this particular decision of his? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may offer my comments on this document, the second paragraph is not in -- is not translated correctly. It speaks of ARM national headquarters. In fact, there was no such thing as ARM national headquarters. This document, in its Macedonian version, clearly speaks about the army General Staff and, in fact, specifically about the Chief of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, I'm grateful for that, Mr. Bezruchenko. Concerning my question, do you agree that, as with previous documents and decisions and order of the president, the president request that reporting from the army be made directly to him in relation to this particular decision? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And, if you look perhaps at the bottom of the document, Mr. Bezruchenko.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: If it could be scrolled down somewhat.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Do you agree that this particular decision was dispatched to the Cabinet of the President, as well as the army headquarters, but not the Ministry of Defence. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'd now like to turn to a different part of your report, and we're going come back perhaps to some of those documents if necessary, and that would be chapter 4 of your report, Mr. Bezruchenko, which is devoted to what you call the attack on Ljuboten, 10, 12 August, 2001. It may be found in your report, which is Exhibit P466 at paragraph 481 and following. Is it correct that -- Mr. Bezruchenko, in that part of your report, one may found your -- one may find your views about what you believe happened in or around or in relation to Ljuboten in the days mentioned, 10 to 12 August of 2001? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as based on the available documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is it correct, Mr. Bezruchenko, that in that particular part of your report, apart from one paragraph, paragraph 506 of the report, you have been careful not to mention the role of the president in relation to those events?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in fact, it was not really my intention to deal with this issue, since I was describing the events in Ljuboten.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is it correct, however, Mr. Bezruchenko, that you were aware of the role played by the president in relation to these matters, and that you have carefully set aside the references to the president's role and actions in relation to these matters?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I mentioned, sir, this particular section of my report was based on the available documents which described the situation in and around Ljuboten on these three specific days.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, let's look at the material then. You are aware that, on the 8th and 10th of August of 2001, the NLA organised two mine attacks in, respectively, Karpalak and Ljubotenski Bacila, to which you refer to in your report. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the record, the matters are dealt with in particular in paragraphs 485 of the report, in particular concerning Ljubotenski Bacila and also, inter alia, at paragraph 134 of part five of Mr. Bezruchenko's report. It's at page 41 of part 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Do you recall, Mr. Bezruchenko, being asked a number of questions by the Office of the Prosecutor concerning the incident in Karpalak on the 8th of August, 2001, in relation to a particular document that was shown to you? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which specific document do you mean, Mr. Mettraux?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown what is Exhibit 2D40, please. This is tab 25 of the Prosecution's binder of documents for Mr. Bezruchenko.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Do you recall being shown this document, Mr. Bezruchenko?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And do you recall being asked a number of questions specifically in relation to the Karpalak attack, which is mentioned at paragraph 1 of this document?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're referring to the attack in the location in Karpalak, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And do you recall that when asked by the Office of the Prosecutor what you believed had been the reason for that attack, you said the following: That, in your view, it had been apparently been aimed at cutting the communication road between Skopje and Tetovo and deny the army the ability to bring re-supply. That is page 6116. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But, in fact, from the review of the material which you had made, Mr. Bezruchenko, you knew that the reason for this attack was quite different. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, strictly speaking in military sense, from the military point of view, I do not really see any other reason for this attack rather than cutting the communication between Tetovo and Skopje. If you mean there were any other reason, perhaps of political nature, this is a entirely different matter, and I really didn't deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But isn't the situation, Mr. Bezruchenko, that by giving such a military-like explanation for what happened, you are, in fact, trying to give a sort of military legitimacy to what, in fact, was a purely criminal undertaking. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Mettraux, my report deals with military issues and such. As I mentioned to you previously, I think on the very first day of the testimony, the criminal aspects, the crimes and all related issues, have not been the subject of my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown what is Rule 65 ter 353.18, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, do you recall reviewing that document in the course of the preparation of your report?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, do you recall relying, inter alia, on the statement of Mr. Peter Matthiesen to prepare your original report?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And do you recall this particular document being one of the annex to Mr. Matthiesen's statement?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps, I'm not sure, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, we'll just go through it slowly. This is a document which, as indicated, comes from the German authority through Mr. Matthiesen, and it's dated the 8th of August of 2001. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And if you go further down the document, you will see that the author of that document is, in fact, identified as Lieutenant-Colonel Matthiesen. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Can you see that, Mr. Bezruchenko?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please scroll the document down a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: This would be just above the subject heading, if that assists you. There is a --

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And there's a subject heading saying: "Internal security here, Macedonia reference running report." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And in his general comment, Mr. Matthiesen says the following: "The country's security situation is deteriorating. An army convoy run into an ambush near Grupcin," which is the incident we have just seen. "The National Liberation Army marches into Tetovo. At least nine soldiers have been killed so far." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And if you can go to the next paragraph -- or the next section which is entitled "Particulars of the situation," Mr. Matthiesen says this: "As a act of revenge for the emptying of an arms catch in Skopje, which left five NLA fighters dead, including the NLA brigadier responsible for Skopje, the Skopje NLA brigade ambushed an army convoy near Grupcin, (route Skopje-Tetovo), at around 0945. Nine soldiers died on the spot." Do you recall reading that particular part of the document, Mr. Bezruchenko?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But, in fact, what it makes clear is that the criminal attack in Grupcin-Karpalak was an act of revenge for the killing of five NLA members in Skopje, including Mr. Teli? Is that correct that's what the document suggests?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's right. This is what the document suggests.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And if can we turn briefly to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Just trying to understand, in the last question, the reference to a "criminal attack," does that come from the evidence or is that Mr. Mettraux's conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Would you wish me to respond, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: It was indeed from my question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That doesn't answer the question. Are you saying it's your interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if the question or IF the clarification of Mr. Saxon is to the effect that it is our position, we can say, yes. And if the further question of Mr. Saxon is that the evidence will support this, we believe it will be the case and we would present a number of documents to that effect to Mr. Bezruchenko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, but I just don't think the matter ends there. It is also a question of fairness to the witness and to the record. That question makes a presumption to the witness that this was a criminal attack, as opposed to another kind of event, and I just think that, in fairness to the witness, he needs to be able to know that he can respond to that, or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I suspect, Mr. Saxon, that the witness is well aware that this is a question based upon a view expressed by one person who was a observer, a military attache of another nation, in which that attache has expressed a view. Neither the Chamber nor the witness are in a position to know the basis for that view, simply from this document, . The witness. I'm sure, from all that he has illustrated over the past several days, is well capable of making that sort of point where he see it is relevant and necessary. So I don't think there's need for any special caution. Please continue, Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Bezruchenko.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Could the registry please turn to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I will ask to you focus your attention on what is paragraph 4 of that document. It is called "measures." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And the advice that Mr. Matthiesen is giving to his government is as follows: "Our urgent vision is to condemn NLA attacks in the press and in the media, most severely." Do you agree that is his advice?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is his advice.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And do you agree that from the material, which you have reviewed in the course of the preparation of your report and the course of your work, the Macedonian authorities and the Macedonian population generally were shocked by these -- this attack in Karpalak, in which nine soldiers died?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it received a wide media coverage.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is that correct also that in your evidence in-chief, you told the Chamber that this incident in Karpalak was the main reason behind what you called the -- or was the main reason -- immediate reason for the resignation of the Chief of the General Staff? That's page 6117. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And that person would be General Petrovski. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But, in fact, Mr. Petrovski did not resign from his position but, as you know -- or I'm putting to you that you know that he was, in fact, relieved of his duties. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And, in fact, you also knew that he had been relieved of his duties by the president of the republic as a result of the incident in Karpalak. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there are various interpretations of this fact. The media reported about these things, at least some media, I think, as resignation. Documents, in fact, suggested that this was indeed dismissal by the president.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, I'm putting it to you, Mr. Bezruchenko, that not only were you fully aware that this was a matter of relief of duty and not resignation, but that for the reason for to you suggest that it was resignation was to hide the direct involvement of the president in the matter of Karpalak and Ljubotenski Bacila. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see any reason why should I hide something like direct involvement of the president, as you put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Do you recall being present during the interview of Mr. Buckovski.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Do you recall Mr. Buckovski saying, and I quote: "The reason for his dismissal," that's General Petrovski, "was the NLA attack at Karpalak where ten armed members were killed." Do you recall him telling you that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a long timing that I reviewed that particular document or I had this meeting, but I think it was also discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And do you recall Mr. Buckovski making that particular point to you? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but I think it was discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, then, could the witness please be shown Rule 65 ter 1D856.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Do you recognise the record of interview of Mr. Buckovski?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And if the registry could please turn to paragraph 15 of that particular document, please, that would be on the third page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And if you can look at the sentence which starts on the fifth line of that particular paragraph, it says that: "The reason for his dismissal was the NLA attack at Karpalak where ten ARM members were killed." Does that help refresh your memory?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Could the witness also be shown what is Rule 65 ter 256, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Do you recall reviewing that statement of General Stambolski?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And if I can ask to you focus on the first paragraph of that document, it says the following: "On 12 August 2001, at around 0830 hours, in the capacity of deputy chief of the army, General Staff, and at the same time as the acting Chief of the ARM General Staff," and then a parenthesis which is the point of me showing you this document. It says this: "Pursuant to the decree dated 10 August 2001 and issued by the president of the Republic of Macedonia, General Pande Petrovski was relieved of his duties and no replacement was point the, and, therefore, he continued to be present in the Cabinet of the Chief of General Staff." Does that also help refresh your memory about the fact that Mr. Petrovski had been relieved of his duties?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The point is that, of course, he was no longer the Chief of General Staff, at least formally.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And isn't that correct that you yourself asked specific questions about the circumstances in which Mr. Petrovski had been relieved of his duties from Mr. Mitrovski during your interview of that person?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is it correct that in addition to relieving Mr. -- or General Petrovski of his duties, the president of the Republic of Macedonia, Mr. Trajkovski, took other steps to respond to what happened in Karpalak and Ljubotenski Bacila?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a very general question, Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, are you aware of any other steps taken by the president to respond to what had happened in Karpalak and Ljubotenski Bacila, anything he did?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any specific steps taken?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to the best of my recollection, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Do you recall being told or do you recall reviewing material which suggested that the president considered these two incidents as humiliating for him as president?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Do you recall reviewing documents or being told by interviewees that the president felt he could not sign the Ohrid Framework Agreement without a response to what happened in Karpalak and Ljubotenski Bacila?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe this whole situation about these two incidents was indeed a matter of discussion with Mr. Buckovski. I don't really recall the exact expression that he used, but I think what transpired from this meeting, among other things, was that, indeed, this was kind of humiliating situation for Macedonian army, and, in fact, this is also the view which is expressed, I think, in the book, "The War in Macedonia," by three Macedonian authors.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And do you recall also that in the material that you reviewed, or during the interviews of people that you had, that the president felt he had to react before the signing of the Ohrid Framework Agreement, that he had to take steps to respond to those attacks?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I mentioned, Mr. Mettraux, this matter was a discussion -- this matter was discussed during our interview with Mr. Buckovski; but if your question is specifically referring to any other interviews in which this issue was discussed, I just cannot tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, let's take it one step at a time then. Do you recall that on the 8th of August, shortly after the first of the two attacks, the attacks in Karpalak, the Macedonian Security Council, also sometimes called the Defence Council, issued a communique condemning the attack in Karpalak? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think such communique was issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And perhaps, for assistance, I would like the registry to bring up Rule 65 ter 1D932, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: There is a press report provided to us by the Office of the Prosecutor, which relates to that particular communique. The title is "FYROM Security Council convenes 10 August, support, firm action." I would like to read out to you what it says. "The Security Council of the Republic of Macedonia held a meeting which focussed on the country's current security and political situation and which resulted in the adoption of a number of specific conclusions. The Security Council paid tribute to the Macedonian security forces's servicemen who were killed near the Skopje village of Ljubanci and expressed deep regret and sympathy to their families. "At last night's meeting, the council concluded that the firm action should resume to eliminate any threat to the security forces and to the citizens of the Republic of Macedonia." Do you recall seeing this document, Mr. Bezruchenko.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think have I seen this document, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is it correct, furthermore, that in the course of the interviews, the various interviews to which you participated, you came to know that the Security Council, or Defence Counsel as we've seen in it occasion, was a body that did not have the power to take any decisions or issue orders? Do you recall being told that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: My impression is the Security Council did not really have any executive authorities, but, of course, this fact did not really prevent the Security Council from making recommendations and issuing communiques.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is this correct, Mr. Bezruchenko -- I'm grateful for your answer, Mr. Bezruchenko. Is it correct that you were told both by Mr. Mitrovski and Mr. Buckovski that the council did not have, as you put, executive powers. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember exactly how they put it, but I think this was discussed and this is the impression that I picked up.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And perhaps I will read to you a passage, again, from the interview of Mr. Buckovski, if that helps refresh your memory. He said the following: "Key decisions were not made at the Security Council sessions. These sessions were used only for political bickerings. There were no records of the Security Council session made. It is pointless to look for them. There were only statements for the media." Do you recall him telling you that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And do you remember that in the course of that same interview, Mr. Buckovski, the former Minister of Defence, was asked specifically about the communique which we have just discussed, and he specified or he made it clear to you that there had been no decision taken in relation to these actions which are mentioned in the communique? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And perhaps to help refresh your memory, I will read the passage from the statement. It says this: "Being shown a media report dated 10 August 2001, and saying that the Security Council session promised'tough action against terrorists,' I say that it was an empty threat. No specific decision related to 'tough action' was made by this session." Do you recall Mr. Buckovski telling you this?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now that you are reading this, yes, I remember this.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And there's another document, Mr. Bezruchenko, that I would like to show you at this moment, and this is Rule 65 ter 1D929.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, perhaps if we can go for a few seconds in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There is a technical delay in going into private session, Mr. Mettraux. We will be informed the moment that is offer.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: It can be done later, Your Honour, the private session part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: If the document, Rule 65 ter 1D929 could be shown to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, this is a document dated the 14th -- sorry, the 10th of August of 2001. Its subject matter is "Macedonia." And if you look at the very bottom of the page, please, the summary is: "Farewell call on Trajkovski. He intends to go on with signature of Framework Agreement on 134 August." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see this specific sentence, but it is not entirely clear what kind of document it is, since most of it has been blackened out.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Bezruchenko, we will do that in a private session when techniques is with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Can we please turn to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'd like to draw your attention, Mr. Bezruchenko, to paragraph 3 of that particular document. It records the following: "I paid a farewell call on president who was in somber mood. He said that he fully intended to continue with signature of the Framework Agreement on 13 August. That and NATO deployment were the only hope. He ascribed the present fighting to a NLA desire to establish new lines of control and an effective partition line before NATO arrived. "I asked him about the phrase 'energetic defensive action' in the national Security Council communique of 8 August. Had this been wise? "He said that the only intent was to get the NLA out of positions which were new since the cease-fire of 6 July. The Macedonians would respect the cease-fire, but it would be impossible to sell the Framework Agreement to parliament while the NLA were continuing to push forward without any response from the army or police." First, let me ask you this, Mr. Bezruchenko: Had you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Would you agree, however, that the passage that I've read to you, aside from the farewell visit is some of the material which you have reviewed in the course of your preparation?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think some points in paragraph 3, in fact, reflect on the situation as was described in various documents that I have reviewed and would be consistent can such description; for example, the point regarding the NLA pushing hard, I think, is certainly a valid one. The NLA was indeed pushing forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is also correct that another matter which is consistent with the material that you reviewed is the fact that the president thought that a response from the army or the police was necessary? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember seeing a document which suggested that the army and the police should respond. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And perhaps we can go into private session for a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, do you recall being told that the attack in Ljubotenski Bacila by the NLA was a convenient occasion for the president to demonstrate his authority before the signing of the Ohrid Framework Agreement?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this was the point which was made by Mr. Buckovski, but I'm not entirely certain if he put it exactly this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, let me read the relevant three sentences from the statement which may assist you. Mr. Buckovski told you that: "There was a sense of humiliation after Karpalak attack. Even president's advisors advised him that signing of the Ohrid Framework Agreement should coincide in time with some sort of military victory. Ljubotenski Bacila was a convenient occasion to demonstrate force." Do you remember Mr. Buckovski telling you this?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this is the exact quotation from his statement, I think this is exactly the fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And, perhaps, you've made that point already; but you will agree that based on the material that you have reviewed in particular, this interview and others, that it was quite clear to you that the president felt, after Karpalak and Ljubotenski Bacila, that he had to respond to the NLA attacks before the signing of the agreement on the 13th of August. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid such an assumption would carry quite a speculative undertones, Mr. Mettraux, because at least for one reason, I have not really seen any documents signed by the president or on his behalf related to any military action, well, in the wake of Karpalak and directly related to Ljuboten.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, I'm putting it to you, Mr. Bezruchenko, that this is it not quite right, and I'm asking this: Do you remember reviewing the statement of Mr. Zlatko Keskovski for the purpose of preparing your report?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I reviewed many statements for the purpose of preparing my report. But if I can bring you back to the point which I've repeatedly made several times, in my final version, in the final version of my report, I was trying hard to rely on firsthand documentary evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is it correct, Mr. Bezruchenko, that in footnote 492, 493, 494, 495, 518, 519, 520, 521, 22, 23, 24, 25, 26, and 27 of your original report, you, in fact, made references to the statement of Mr. Keskovski? I'm talking of your original report.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it would probably give me some time to give you the precise answer, Mr. Mettraux, since I simply have to refer to each and every footnote that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, perhaps, I will assist you. If you can take -- I can see that you have the version of your report that contains the amendments, and I will ask you to turn to page 100 of your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: It's exhibit P466.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And if you can look also at page 101 of your statement which contain the amendments, can you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And you agree that there were four references in those footnotes to the statement of Mr. Zlatko Keskovski of 7 February 2005. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that appears so.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And if you can go now to what is page 106 of the report, do you agree there that there are, again, a number of references to the statements of -- the ICTY statement of 7 February of 2005 of Mr. Zlatko Keskovski?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: So, do you recall now relying in your original report on the statement of that person?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And do you recall Mr. Keskovski, who, at the time was the chief of security of the president of the Republic of Macedonia, telling you that the president was under great pressure to do something, do you recall that, under pressure from the public?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I reviewed his statement, that's right, and I indeed used his statement to substantiate various points in my report, at least in its initial original form. But if the implication of your question is whether I was reflecting the specific role of the president and his feelings and his, well, views, it is not really the purposes of my report. If I could kindly refer, Mr. Mettraux, to the very first page of my report, which clearly states what was the scope and what was -- or rather, what were the original objectives of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But do you agree, Mr. Bezruchenko, that the whole purpose of this section of your report is to provide relevant information to the Chamber about what you say happened in the village during those three days and the circumstances in which these matters evolved and for what reason? Do you agree that was the purpose of part 4?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The purpose of part 4, by and large and primarily, Mr. Mettraux, was to describe the events exactly as they happened on the ground, and as based in various documents. And while reviewing these documents, I did not really see any direct strong evidence indicating that the president was directly involved in the events of Ljuboten.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, we're going to --

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, there was some circumstantial evidence suggesting that perhaps he was consulted by one of the military officers of the Macedonian army, regarding the support to be provided for the police forces in the area of Ljuboten, but this is only circumstantial evidence which was reflected in a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, I'm putting to you, Mr. Bezruchenko, that what you in fact did in your report is to positively hide the fact of the involvement of the president in those events. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in order for me to hide this fact, Mr. Mettraux, I should have known well in advance what kind of direct involvement it was, which particular fact it had been manifested in, and what kind of documents this evidence would have been supported.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: For instance, Mr. Bezruchenko, and contrary to the evidence you gave a moment ago, you had material indicating to you that the sense of humiliation, which you acknowledge was felt, inter alia, by the president, and the actions, which he was advised and felt he had to take, directly related to the events of Ljuboten. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid what we are missing in this statement of yours, Mr. Mettraux, is a link between the mental state and the actual act. I do not see any documents suggesting that this feeling was reflected in any particular order by the document -- or by the president.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Can the witness please be shown what is Rule 65 ter 1D526, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Perhaps before I ask you this, I will ask you a general question Mr. Bezruchenko. Is it correct that the president of the Republic of Macedonia is dead.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is it correct also that the president of the Republic of Macedonia died sometime in February of 2004?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I recall correctly, yes, this unfortunate air crash took place in February 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And is it correct also that the death of the president occurred prior to most of the interviews of suspects and witnesses which you've conducted in this case?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be the fair assumption perhaps, but I don't really understand what it has to do with and what the president's death has to do with my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, just staying with the question for a second, do you agree that most of the Prosecution's statements and interviews took place after the early death of the president? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The analysis as to the timings and locations of the interview was not really my undertaking, Mr. Mettraux. So I can honestly tell you that I was not thinking whether these interviews were taking after the president's death or before that and how it really reflected on my presentation of the material confined in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, let's look at this document then. This is the record of interview or the statement of Mr. Keskovski, Zlatko taken by the Office of the Prosecutor. It is dated the 7th of February of 2005. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And if it could be scrolled down a bit for Mr. Bezruchenko.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Do you agree, Mr. Bezruchenko?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that the date of this specific statement. This is a statement, Mr. Mettraux, not a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'm grateful for that.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is dated 7 February 2005.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Mr. Bezruchenko.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Could the registry please turn to page 9 of this document. That would be 1D00-4780. And if the registry to please focus on the last paragraph on that page, that would be paragraph 40.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, I'll ask you to locate a sentence which is five lines from the bottom of that paragraph, paragraph 40, which starts with the word: "The major replied." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And Mr. Keskovski is talking, as is evident from the previous paragraph in the content of his statement, from a phone call between a major, Major Despodov, and the president; and Mr. Keskovski recounts the following: "The major replied that the president was his supreme superior, and he would have to obey the order from the president. In that period of time, the president was under pressure from the public because he was thought to have failed to use the army appropriately in dealing with the terrorists; therefore, he wanted to speak to the major." Do you agree, Mr. Bezruchenko, that at least as far as the statement of Mr. Keskovski is concerned, there is a pretty clear link, and a pretty direct one with that, between the pressure which the president was under from the public at the time to do something and his actions vis-a-vis the events of Ljuboten? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: My interpretation of this statement would be somewhat different, Mr. Mettraux. But before actually I provide my interpretation, I would like to -- I would like to you refer to section 4 of my report, specifically to the paragraph in which I mention, in fact, that Major Despodov, indeed, apparently had a phone conversation with the president. So this fact, the fact of this conversation, was, indeed, reflected in my report. Now let me comment on this particular paragraph. What I see here is, indeed, a reflection on the mental state of the president; and, apparently, he shared the widespread sense of humiliation which actually hit the Macedonian public and society in the following -- in the wake of the Karpalak attack, which is obvious for many media sources. Well, whether there was a actual order given in relation to Ljuboten by the president, I cannot really tell, because, first of all, this paragraph doesn't really specify it, it doesn't say so; and, second, I really have not seen any documents, any order signed by the president in relation to Ljuboten which would support the opinion expressed in this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you this, Mr. Bezruchenko: Is it correct that you have seen other documents which, in fact, make it clear to you that the operation in Ljuboten was ordered by the president? Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you show me such a document, I would be grateful, Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'm going to show documents in a second, Mr. Bezruchenko, but do you recall seeing any such documents?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Documents signed by the president directly mentioning Ljuboten?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: No, Mr. Bezruchenko. I'm referring to a document that refer to the fact that the operation in Ljuboten had been ordered by the president.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Mettraux, with all my due respect, may I indicate to you that we are apparently talking about different things. I already mentioned to you a number of times that I have not seen any documents signed by the president dealing with the operation, as you term it, in Ljuboten. You seem to suggest, in fact, that I have seen such documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: No, I apologise, Mr. Bezruchenko, if my questions came across as a suggestion of a document signed by the president. What I'm asking you is whether you saw documents which were not signed by the president, which were authored by other people, which made it clear to you that the operation in Ljuboten had been ordered by the president. Have you seen any such documents?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly have seen some witness statements; but documents specifically mentioning in direct terms that this operation was ordered by the president, no, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Do you recall --

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Would it be a convenient time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I thought you were about to move into a treatment of specific documents, in which event it would be more convenient to break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could Mr. Bezruchenko please be shown what is Exhibit P304, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, do you recall seeing this document in the course of your preparation?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And this is a report prepared by Mr. Blazo Kopacev, and it is dated the 12th of August, 2001. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And looking at this first page, there is a first paragraph; and at the end of the paragraph, it says that Mr. Despodov was informed about the mission which no one should know of except the above mentioned persons. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And if I can draw your attention to the next paragraph, it says this: "The action about which none was supposed to know on the order of the president was supposed to begin on 11 August 2001 at 4.30. For a unknown reason, the action did not begin." Do you agree that this document suggests that the president had given orders in relation to this particular operation -- action?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, obviously, this is your interpretation of this document, Mr. Mettraux. But with all my due respect, I don't really see any hard facts here suggesting that the president ordered this operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Do you recall --

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you see, this sentence is actually from a linguistic point even, if I may say so, written in subjunctive mood, which suggests a supposition rather than an actual fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Do you recall reading also, Mr. Bezruchenko, so that Mr. Despodov at the time was given a guarantee that he would be personally protected by the president? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Guarantee by whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: By --

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, we can turn to the third page of the document then.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And if I can draw your attention to the last paragraph, and in particular the last seven or eight words of that paragraph, can you see that there's a reference to the fact that he would be protected personally by the president. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Mettraux, I'm afraid you did not answer my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Bezruchenko, I'm not here to answer your questions. I think you can look at that paragraph for yourself. Do you agree that what this paragraph suggests, in effect, is that the -- Mr. Despodov, the commander to whom reference is made, is being told that he would be protected personally by the president? Is that correct? It's the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Mettraux, in order for me to understand the full implication of your questions, I would kindly ask you to answer my previous question.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Bezruchenko, can you see the last paragraph on that document which starts with the word: "Finally"?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see this paragraph, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And are you able to read it?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And are you able to understand the content of that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And do you agree that in the last few words of that particular paragraph, there's a indication to the effect that Mr. Despodov would be protected personally by the president. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: What it says here - may I read to you out, loud Mr. Mettraux: For that, he received guarantees from Johan Tarculovski that he would not bear any responsibility for the action, and he would be protected personally by the president."

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And what this means in practice, Mr. Bezruchenko, I hope you can agree with that, is that the authority which was being exercised was the authority of the president. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's really difficult for me to understand what you mean, Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, do you agree that the guarantee that was given to Mr. Despodov was to the effect that the president would protect him in case there would be any problems?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what the document says.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And the authority, therefore, on which this guarantee is based is that of the president, is that correct, based on this document again?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And do you recall also that you asked General Mitrovski about this particular document? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And if the registry could please bring up what I believe is Rule 65 ter 2D310. I apologise, this is just a summary of the interview. I'd like the interview itself, which would be Rule 65 ter 1D936.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, that is, again, the record of interview of Mr. Sokol Mitrovski, and it is dated the 1st of August of 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And I will ask the registry, please, to go to page 56 of that interview. This is page 1D00-7964, and if we can scroll down a little bit to the bottom of the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'd like to read out to you, Mr. Bezruchenko, a question that you asked of Mr. Mitrovski. You said this: "One last question in connection with," missing word, "when the investigation is completed and when the report is received," and there's a part missing. "When you received the report from Colonel Kopacek," it should be Kopacev," what was your analysis of this report and what action did you take on it?"

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: If we can turn to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And there is the answer of General Sokol Mitrovski: "I was -- I only wanted to know if the Chief of the General Staff and the Minister were familiar with this. When they said they were, for me that was a done job. They were supposed to see, analyse this, and decide whether they should speak with the president. I didn't have such competencies." Do you agree that what Mr. Mitrovski told you, and what is clear from his answer, is that the military hierarchy was aware that the person to whom they should turn, if they should turn to anyone to obtain a explanation about what happened, was to the president? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: My interpretation of this paragraph would be somewhat different, Mr. Mettraux. May I read this paragraph to you again: "I only wanted to know if the Chief of the General Staff and the Minister were familiar with this. When they said they were, for me it was a done job. They were supposed to see, analysis this, and decide whether they should speak with the president. I did not have such competencies." What is very clear from this paragraph is apparently that Mr. Mitrovski's actions stopped at the level of the General Staff, and he was not aware of what was going to happen and if it was going to happen at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But do you agree that what it also refers to and acknowledged is that the fact, as you point out, if there was something to talk further up the chain of command, ultimately that would be the president that he pointed to? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is very logical to assume.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But the reason for that is even more logical, Mr. Bezruchenko, because Mr. Mitrovski himself had talked to the president directly during that weekend. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: They may have had an exchange, if I recall, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And, in fact, that is what Mr. Mitrovski explained to you during the interview. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you can show me this portion of the interview, I can probably confirm it.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, if we can turn to the next page, and if we can --

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: If you can start at line 7, Mr. Bezruchenko, it starts with the word: I contacted." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And it says: "I contacted, I had contacts with the president very rarely. I think there was one phone call from the president but nothing concrete was discussed. As far as I remember, he asked me about my position. I said, 'I'm the commander.' I don't remember that there was no order, no request for me to go to him. I think he only showed interest in the general situation after the events, nothing more." Then there's a discussion that follows between Mr. Kuehnel and the general, in particular as to the date of this conversation, which Mitrovski is not sure about; and then on the next page, he indicates that the discussion also had to do with Ljuboten. Do you recall him telling you that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Ljuboten was discussed of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But there's another matter which you knew, Mr. Bezruchenko, at the time of preparing your report, and that's the report of Mr. Kostadinov.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And if the witness could now be shown what is now Exhibit P303, please.

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may suggest, Mr. Mettraux, before we actually come over to this specific document, I would like to finish my comment about the previous interview; and perhaps for this reason, you can kindly go to the previous page of the interview, line 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Can the record of interview be shown once again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I kindly draw your attention, Mr. Mettraux, to line 11 of this particular document, which clearly says: "I don't remember that there was no order, no request for me to go to him."

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Yes. There was no order for Mr. Mitrovski to go to the president. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no order. Whether there was an order to go to him or to do anything else in relation to the situation, there was simply no order.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But that's your interpretation, isn't it, Mr. Bezruchenko, the interpretation which you've tried to put all over your report. This sentence, Mr. Bezruchenko, says this: "I don't remember that there was no order, no request for me to go to him." Is that correct that's what the sentence says?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my reading of this, Mr. Mettraux, is that there was no order.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, let me put it to you, Mr. Bezruchenko, that this reading of the sentence reflects your reading of the entire material which you have reviewed and which you have interpreted, I'm putting it to you, with a view to hide the involvement of the president. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I cannot really agree with you, Mr. Mettraux, for one simple reason. As I mentioned previously, I think I mentioned the fact of discussion of the situation in Ljuboten between Major Despodov and the president in my report. However, I don't really think that this particular fact, the fact of the discussion, would deserve more attention in my report and should be mentioned in more than one paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And is it correct, Mr. Bezruchenko, that at the time when you interviewed Mr. Mitrovski, in August of 2004, the president was dead already? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And if we can now move to Exhibit P303, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: This, again, Mr. Bezruchenko, is a report with which you would be quite familiar. This is a report prepared by Mr. Kostadinov. It is dated the 12th of August of 2001, and its subject is "Report on actions and situation in the 3rd Guardist Brigade, village Ljuboten." Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And if I can draw your attention to the first paragraph which starts with the words: "On 10 August." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And I will ask to you locate a sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And if the registry can assist a little bit by scrolling down in the document.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The interpreters kindly ask the witness to pause before answering questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko, I would like to ask to locate a sentence, which is five or so lines from the bottom of the first paragraph, starting started with the word "Major Despodov." Can you see that [check].

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And the report says the following: "Major Despodov asked them on whose order they had come. They said that this is known to the president, and no one else should know about their stay. Major Despodov asked them what their role is here. They answered that they had the task to enter in the village Ljuboten and to conduct a search and cleaning of the terrain." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And, first, let me ask you this: Did you refer to this particular passage of the report anywhere in your report, Mr. Bezruchenko?

utterances.speaker: VIKTOR BEZRUCHENKO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this document is widely quoted in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
